correctness_findings.claim: lineage_detail string still says "but peer's latest position has no such claim_id" — but after the fix, peer_prior is the peer's round-(N-1) snapshot, not 'latest'. This text is persisted into verifier_ledger.json and consumed by synthesis/retro tooling, so any fabricated_peer_ref that does fire will mis-describe what was compared.

round_num==1 branch hardcodes peer_prior={'claims': []} and ignores any data in prior_positions_by_agent. If verify_round is ever invoked with round_num=1 but a populated prior dict (replay/resume, retro_verify scripts, future graph that pre-seeds peer state), legitimate peer claim_ids are discarded and every reference is flagged fabricated. The branch is selected purely on round_num rather than on whether the dict actually has data.

prior_positions_by_agent.get(peer_name) or {'claims': []} is asymmetric with own_prior handling on line 599 (left as None). Missing own_prior silently skips silent_rename/silent_retire (line 512 guard); missing peer_prior is materialized to an empty position and forces fabricated_peer_ref to fire for every reference. No justification given for opposite defaults on symmetric halves of the same dict — a state inconsistency dropping one agent's entry produces a flood of false fabrications while silently ignoring the symmetric own-lineage case.

test_lineage_detects_fabricated_peer_ref passes prior_positions_by_agent={}, so peer_prior resolves to {'claims': []} under the new code. Under the OLD code peer_prior would have been latest_positions[agent_b] which contained b1; b99 is fabricated either way. Neither path exercises the rename-induced false positive (peer's prior had b1, peer's latest renamed it to b1_v2, agent agreed to b1). A future revert to latest_positions[peer] would still pass this test, so the suite does not guard against the regression the commit claims to fix.

Same gap as line 251: test_lineage_detects_fabricated_disagreement_target also uses prior_positions_by_agent={} and passes under either dispatch. No test in the file constructs the specific scenario the fix addresses (peer's prior snapshot contains the referenced claim_id while peer's latest position has renamed it). The commit message brags 'Tests unchanged ... same semantics' which is precisely the regression risk.

nits.claim: Comment block on lines 624-629 largely restates the explanation from lines 601-612; could be collapsed.

_detect_fabricated_peer_refs docstring (lines 480-486) says callers 'must pass an empty dict (not None) for the round-1 case under the barrier' but the function still accepts None and returns []. The 'must' is a caller-side contract enforced only by verify_round; any other caller (retro scripts, future graph wiring) that passes None for round 1 will silently produce zero fabrications instead of the intended behavior.

scope_drift_findings: Empirical claims in the commit message about v1=4, v2=6 cross-leak counts and the cascade-vs-barrier counterfactual ('would have been 7 false positives without the fix') are not reproducibly demonstrated by anything in the commit diff itself — they require running both code paths against the same v3 trace, which the diff does not provide.
summary: The fix is directionally correct: routing peer_prior through prior_positions_by_agent for round_num>=2 matches what the barrier guarantees agents actually saw, and the retro v3 ledger confirms fabricated_peer_ref=0 / silent_retire=7. However, real issues remain. (1) The lineage_detail message in _lineage_entries still says "peer's latest position has no such claim_id" — under the fix the comparison is against the peer's PRIOR snapshot, not "latest"; this stale message ships into verifier_ledger.json and downstream synthesis. (2) The author's claim "Tests unchanged ... same semantics" is the problem itself: the two fabricated_peer_ref tests pass prior_positions_by_agent={}, so peer_prior resolves to {'claims': []} under both old and new code. Neither test exercises the actual bug being fixed (peer renamed claim_ids so latest disagrees with prior); a revert to latest_positions[peer] would still pass the suite. (3) Asymmetric defensive handling: missing own_prior remains None (silent skip), missing peer_prior is materialized to {'claims': []} (forces fabrication firing). The round_num==1 branch unconditionally discards any populated prior_positions_by_agent, coupling correctness to one scheduling assumption.
